(CNN) -- From the world's biggest manufacturer of mobile phone batteries to a car company with global pretensions, BYD is a Chinese company that has roared onto the international stage energized by its workaholic founder Wang Chuanfu. Building his own dreams: Wang Chuanfu has turned BYD into an international company in less than 15 years. Wang's hands-on approach to running a business with 130,000 employees  -- he still eats in the company canteen and lives in a BYD-owned housing complex -- isn't too far removed from how he built the company from scratch in 1995 when he was 29 years old. Wang trained as an engineer and studied the patents of other companies' mobile phone batteries, even taking them apart to see how they were made. He raised some start-up capital from a relative to create his own mobile phone battery-making business in Shenzhen, the special economic zone just north of Hong Kong. BYD's business approach differed from the likes of Sony and Sanyo by substituting an automated system for one of China's biggest resources, physical labor. Employing thousands of people was cheaper than installing expensive robotic assembly lines, and by 2000 BYD had become the biggest mobile phone battery maker in the world. Wang bought a failing Chinese car company in 2003 to enter the automobile market, and BYD now has a number of models available in China, including a plug-hybrid car cheaper than the market-leading Toyota Prius. The success of BYD has attracted plenty of attention from industry analysts and investors from the West, including Warren Buffet. The billionaire American has invested $250 million in BYD, making even more people in the West sit up and take note of the company. Wang isn't content to just compete in the hybrid and electric car market in China; he aims to keep BYD's meteoric rise going and make it the world's biggest car maker by 2025. "It is a big ambition. In January and February 2009 China was the world's biggest automobile consuming market for those months. So based on this, China can sell more than 10 million automobiles this year. So maybe China can exceed the USA and become the biggest market in the world," Wang told CNN. BYD stands for "Build Your Dreams" and Wang is trying to fulfill the aspiration among many in China of creating a national champion; a brand with international respect and reputation of quality. Wang believes the electric car can be that product, and BYD the company to do it. "For new energy vehicles...China is on the same level or even leading other countries. In the field of new energy cars, China hopes that Chinese companies can catch up with the rest of the world and catch up with the pace," said Wang. But the term "Made in China" still has a stigma attached to it. The scandals of tainted milk and toys that had to be recalled rocked China in 2008 and diminished the reputation of Chinese products abroad. "This kind of 'Made in China' is different from other types of 'Made in China.' Our products have never been recalled, unlike many of our competitors. Judging from that, products made in China are sometimes better that those made elsewhere. As long as there are high-standards, Chinese manufacturing companies can definitely meet those standards," said Wang. China also has acute environmental problems. It is the world's biggest emitter of greenhouse gases and Wang is aware that being an entrepreneur also means having an eye on the environmental impact of his business. "As an entrepreneur, I think I have to consider both aspects. One part is the creation of a new business mode, or the revelation of new business competition. The other is that it's for social responsibility, making our Earth bluer. "Urban pollution, reliance on petroleum and emission of carbon dioxide are three problems that entrepreneurs have to consider for basic social responsibility," said Wang.

(CNN) -- From the world’s largest manufacturer of mobile phone batteries to an automaker with global ambitions, BYD is a Chinese company that has surged onto the international stage, driven by the energy and work ethic of its founder, Wang Chuanfu.

Building his own dreams, Wang Chuanfu has transformed BYD into an international company in less than 15 years. His hands-on approach to running a business with 130,000 employees—he still eats in the company canteen and lives in a BYD-owned housing complex—is not far removed from the way he built the company from the ground up in 1995, when he was 29 years old.

Trained as an engineer, Wang studied the patents of other companies’ mobile phone batteries, even taking them apart to understand how they were made. He raised start-up capital from a relative to establish his own mobile phone battery manufacturing business in Shenzhen, the special economic zone just north of Hong Kong.

BYD’s business model differed from those of companies such as Sony and Sanyo by replacing automated systems with one of China’s most abundant resources: manual labor. Employing thousands of people was cheaper than installing expensive robotic assembly lines, and by 2000, BYD had become the world’s largest maker of mobile phone batteries.

In 2003, Wang acquired a struggling Chinese car company to enter the automobile market. BYD now offers several models in China, including a plug-in hybrid car that is cheaper than the market-leading Toyota Prius.

BYD’s success has attracted considerable attention from industry analysts and Western investors, including Warren Buffett. The American billionaire has invested $250 million in BYD, prompting even more people in the West to take notice of the company.

Wang is not content merely to compete in China’s hybrid and electric car market; he aims to sustain BYD’s meteoric rise and make it the world’s largest automaker by 2025.

“It is a big ambition. In January and February 2009, China was the world’s biggest automobile consuming market for those months. So based on this, China can sell more than 10 million automobiles this year. So maybe China can exceed the USA and become the biggest market in the world,” Wang told CNN.

BYD stands for “Build Your Dreams,” and Wang is seeking to fulfill an aspiration shared by many in China: to create a national champion—a brand with international respect and a reputation for quality. Wang believes the electric car can be that product, and BYD the company to deliver it.

“For new energy vehicles... China is on the same level or even leading other countries. In the field of new energy cars, China hopes that Chinese companies can catch up with the rest of the world and catch up with the pace,” Wang said.

Yet the phrase “Made in China” still carries a stigma. The scandals involving tainted milk and recalled toys shook China in 2008 and damaged the reputation of Chinese products abroad.

“This kind of ‘Made in China’ is different from other types of ‘Made in China.’ Our products have never been recalled, unlike many of our competitors. Judging from that, products made in China are sometimes better than those made elsewhere. As long as there are high standards, Chinese manufacturing companies can definitely meet those standards,” Wang said.

China also faces acute environmental challenges. It is the world’s largest emitter of greenhouse gases, and Wang recognizes that being an entrepreneur also means considering the environmental impact of his business.

“As an entrepreneur, I think I have to consider both aspects. One part is the creation of a new business mode, or the revelation of new business competition. The other is that it’s for social responsibility, making our Earth bluer.

“Urban pollution, reliance on petroleum and emission of carbon dioxide are three problems that entrepreneurs have to consider for basic social responsibility,” Wang said.

The name BYD means “Build Your Dreams,” and Wang is seeking to realize a goal shared by many in China: the creation of a national champion, a brand recognized internationally for both prestige and quality. He sees electric vehicles as the product that can achieve this, and BYD as the company capable of delivering it.

“For new energy vehicles...China is on the same level or even leading other countries. In the field of new energy cars, China hopes that Chinese companies can catch up with the rest of the world and catch up with the pace,” Wang said.

“This kind of ‘Made in China’ is different from other types of ‘Made in China.’ Our products have never been recalled, unlike many of our competitors. Judging from that, products made in China are sometimes better that those made elsewhere. China also faces severe environmental challenges. It is the world’s largest emitter of greenhouse gases, and Wang recognizes that entrepreneurship must include concern for the environmental consequences of business activity.

“As an entrepreneur, I think I have to consider both aspects. One part is the creation of a new business mode, or the revelation of new business competition. The other is that it's for social responsibility, making our Earth bluer.

“Urban pollution, reliance on petroleum and emission of carbon dioxide are three problems that entrepreneurs have to consider for basic social responsibility,” Wang said.

counterfactuals.output:
**BYD’s Wang Chuanfu built a battery empire. Now he wants to take on the world’s carmakers**

When Wang Chuanfu founded BYD in 1995, he was not trying to become a global auto baron. He was trying to make batteries — cheaply, reliably and at scale.

Nearly three decades later, the low-profile Chinese entrepreneur has turned that battery business into one of the world’s most formidable electric vehicle companies, transforming BYD from a supplier for mobile phones into a giant that now competes with Tesla, Volkswagen and Toyota in the race to electrify transportation.

Wang’s rise is a story of engineering discipline, cost control and a willingness to make big bets before the market was ready. It is also a story that drew one of the world’s most famous investors: Warren Buffett.

### From batteries to a manufacturing powerhouse

Born in Anhui province in eastern China, Wang trained as a chemist and researcher before founding BYD — short for “Build Your Dreams” — in Shenzhen, the southern Chinese city that became a symbol of China’s manufacturing boom.

BYD’s first major business was rechargeable batteries, at a time when mobile phones and consumer electronics were exploding in popularity. The company became a major supplier to global handset makers, producing nickel-cadmium and later lithium-ion batteries with a model that emphasized lower-cost production and tight control over its supply chain.

That battery expertise would become BYD’s greatest advantage.

Unlike many automakers that relied heavily on outside suppliers, BYD built much of its core technology in-house. Over time, the company expanded into phone components, electronics assembly, semiconductors, energy storage and eventually automobiles.

The move into cars began in 2003, when BYD acquired a struggling state-owned automaker, Qinchuan Automobile. At the time, the decision surprised many investors. Batteries were already a profitable business; carmaking was capital-intensive, brutally competitive and far outside BYD’s core market.

But Wang saw the future differently. If batteries were going to power phones, laptops and eventually entire energy systems, they could also power cars.

### Buffett’s big bet

In 2008, BYD received a major vote of confidence from Warren Buffett’s Berkshire Hathaway. Through its energy unit, then known as MidAmerican Energy, Berkshire invested about $230 million for a roughly 10% stake in BYD.

The investment was reportedly championed by Charlie Munger, Buffett’s longtime business partner, who admired Wang’s technical ability and BYD’s manufacturing culture.

At the time, BYD was still little known outside China, and electric vehicles were far from mainstream. Tesla had only recently delivered its first Roadsters. Most global automakers treated EVs as a niche or regulatory experiment.

Buffett’s backing gave BYD international credibility — and helped cement Wang’s reputation as one of China’s most serious industrial entrepreneurs.

The bet proved enormously lucrative. As China became the world’s largest EV market and BYD’s sales surged, Berkshire’s stake soared in value, though the firm has since reduced portions of its holdings.

### China’s EV boom changes the game

BYD’s auto business took years to mature. Early models were often criticized for quality and design, and the company struggled at times to convince buyers it could compete with established global brands.

But the arrival of China’s electric vehicle boom changed everything.

Government subsidies, strict emissions rules, rapid charging infrastructure and intense local competition helped create the world’s most dynamic EV market. BYD was well positioned: it had battery technology, manufacturing scale and experience building affordable vehicles for Chinese consumers.

The company’s breakthrough came as it shifted heavily toward “new energy vehicles,” a category in China that includes battery-electric cars and plug-in hybrids. BYD stopped producing purely gasoline-powered cars in 2022, a symbolic move that underscored Wang’s conviction that the future of the industry was electric.

Its proprietary Blade Battery, a lithium iron phosphate battery designed to be safer and cheaper than some rival chemistries, became a key selling point. BYD also benefited from vertical integration, making its own batteries, motors, power electronics and chips — an approach that helped it control costs during global supply chain disruptions.

The result: BYD became China’s top-selling EV maker and one of the largest electric vehicle producers in the world.

### Taking the fight overseas

Wang’s next ambition is global.

BYD has expanded aggressively beyond China, selling passenger cars in markets including Europe, Southeast Asia, Latin America and Australia. It has built a strong presence in electric buses and commercial vehicles as well, with operations in countries from the United States to Brazil.

The company is also investing in overseas production. BYD has announced or pursued manufacturing plans in markets such as Thailand, Brazil, Hungary and other regions as it seeks to reduce trade barriers, localize supply chains and become a truly global carmaker.

That expansion comes with challenges. Chinese EV makers face growing scrutiny from regulators in the United States and Europe, where officials worry about subsidies, market access and competition from lower-cost Chinese imports. In the US passenger car market, tariffs and geopolitical tensions make large-scale entry difficult.

Brand recognition is another hurdle. BYD is a household name in China, but in many overseas markets it must still persuade consumers that a Chinese automaker can match or exceed the quality, safety and reliability of established brands.

Wang appears undeterred. His strategy has been to compete not only on price, but also on technology and scale — offering a wide lineup of EVs and plug-in hybrids aimed at mass-market buyers as well as more premium consumers.

### A quiet engineer in a noisy industry

Unlike some global auto executives, Wang is not known for flamboyance. He is often described as reserved, technical and intensely focused on execution. His public appearances tend to emphasize manufacturing, innovation and long-term planning rather than personal celebrity.

That understated style has helped shape BYD’s culture. The company is known for engineering depth and relentless cost discipline — traits that have allowed it to thrive in China’s cutthroat EV market, where price wars can quickly punish weaker players.

Still, BYD’s rise has made Wang one of the most important figures in the global auto industry. His company represents a broader shift in power: China is no longer just a manufacturing base for foreign carmakers; it is now producing its own global automotive champions.

For decades, the world’s car industry was dominated by American, European, Japanese and South Korean brands. Wang Chuanfu wants BYD to prove that the next era may look very different.

From mobile phone batteries to electric cars, BYD’s journey has followed the arc of China’s industrial transformation. And if Wang succeeds abroad, the company he built in Shenzhen could become one of the defining automakers of the electric age.

---

# From Batteries to Big Ambitions: How Wang Chuanfu Built BYD Into a Global EV Powerhouse

**Shenzhen, China** — When Wang Chuanfu founded BYD in the mid-1990s, the company was not trying to reinvent the automobile. It was trying to make batteries — cheaply, reliably and at scale.

Three decades later, that battery business has become the foundation of one of China’s most closely watched corporate success stories. BYD, short for “Build Your Dreams,” has grown from a rechargeable battery manufacturer into one of the world’s largest electric vehicle makers, challenging legacy automakers and reshaping the global car industry.

At the center of that rise is Wang, a chemist-turned-entrepreneur whose low-profile demeanor contrasts with the company’s increasingly high-profile ambitions.

## A Battery Company First

Wang was born in Anhui province in eastern China and trained as a materials scientist, a background that would become central to BYD’s identity. In 1995, he founded the company in Shenzhen, the southern Chinese city that became a hub for manufacturing, electronics and later electric vehicles.

BYD initially focused on rechargeable batteries for mobile phones and consumer electronics. At a time when global electronics demand was surging, the company became a supplier to major handset makers by finding ways to reduce production costs and scale up quickly.

That early battery expertise gave BYD a crucial advantage when the auto industry began shifting toward electrification. Unlike many carmakers that had to rely on outside suppliers for batteries, BYD already understood chemistry, manufacturing and supply chains.

It was a vertically integrated approach long before that term became fashionable in the EV sector.

## The Leap Into Cars

BYD entered the automotive business in 2003 by acquiring a struggling state-owned car manufacturer. The move surprised some investors and industry observers. Building cars was far more complex than building batteries, and China’s auto market was already crowded with domestic brands and foreign joint ventures.

But Wang saw an opening. China’s growing middle class was buying cars in record numbers, and the government was beginning to view new energy vehicles as a strategic industry — one that could help reduce dependence on imported oil, cut urban pollution and give Chinese companies a chance to compete globally.

BYD’s early gasoline cars were not always praised for design or refinement. But the company kept investing in plug-in hybrids, battery technology and electric drivetrains. Its breakthrough came as the Chinese government poured subsidies, incentives and infrastructure investment into the EV sector.

## Warren Buffett’s Vote of Confidence

One of BYD’s most important moments came in 2008, when a company backed by Warren Buffett’s Berkshire Hathaway bought a stake in BYD. The investment brought international attention and credibility to a company that was still little known outside China.

Buffett’s longtime business partner Charlie Munger later praised Wang as an unusually capable engineer and executive. The endorsement helped turn BYD into a symbol of China’s emerging clean-tech ambitions.

Still, BYD’s path was not linear. The company faced quality concerns, intense competition and periods of investor skepticism. Its early efforts to expand abroad were uneven. But it continued to deepen its technological base, especially in batteries.

## The Blade Battery and Vertical Integration

A major turning point came with BYD’s “Blade Battery,” a lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, battery designed to improve safety and durability while lowering costs. LFP batteries generally have lower energy density than some nickel-based batteries, but they are cheaper, more stable and less reliant on expensive metals such as cobalt and nickel.

That chemistry has become increasingly attractive across the EV industry, especially for mass-market vehicles.

BYD’s strength lies not only in battery chemistry but in its control over much of the supply chain. The company makes its own batteries, electric motors, power electronics and semiconductors. That vertical integration has helped it manage costs and respond quickly to market shifts.

In China’s brutally competitive EV market, where price cuts have become common and new models arrive at a rapid pace, cost control can be decisive.

## Passing Tesla in China — and Competing Globally

BYD’s rise has been especially visible in China, the world’s largest auto market and the global center of EV adoption. The company has become a dominant player in plug-in hybrids and fully electric vehicles, offering a wide range of models from affordable compact cars to premium vehicles.

Its lineup includes mass-market models such as the Dolphin, Seal and Atto 3, as well as vehicles under higher-end sub-brands. BYD’s plug-in hybrid technology has also proved popular with consumers who want lower fuel costs without relying entirely on charging infrastructure.

The company has at times surpassed Tesla in global sales of battery electric vehicles on a quarterly basis, while leading in overall “new energy vehicle” sales when plug-in hybrids are included.

But BYD’s ambitions now extend far beyond China.

The company has expanded into Europe, Southeast Asia, Latin America and other markets. It has announced or explored overseas manufacturing plans in regions including Thailand, Brazil, Hungary and Mexico. Its electric buses are already used in cities around the world.

## A New Challenge: Becoming a Global Automaker

Building cars for the world is different from dominating at home.

Outside China, BYD faces brand recognition challenges, regulatory scrutiny, tariffs, geopolitical tensions and established rivals with deep dealer networks. In Europe, policymakers have investigated Chinese EV subsidies and moved toward tariffs on some imports. In the United States, Chinese automakers face steep political and trade barriers.

There are also questions about whether BYD can match global competitors in software, premium branding and after-sales service — areas increasingly important as cars become connected devices on wheels.

Yet BYD has advantages few rivals can match: scale, battery know-how, aggressive pricing and a vast domestic market that allows rapid product iteration.

Industry analysts say the company’s ability to produce affordable EVs profitably could make it a formidable competitor, particularly in emerging markets where cost matters most.

## Wang’s Low-Key Leadership

Unlike some global auto executives, Wang rarely cultivates a celebrity image. He is often described as technical, disciplined and intensely focused on engineering. That has shaped BYD’s culture: pragmatic, manufacturing-driven and oriented around long-term cost reduction.

The company’s slogan, “Build Your Dreams,” may sound aspirational, but its rise has been built on something more concrete — batteries, supply chains and relentless scale.

Wang’s bet was that the future of cars would be electric, and that the companies controlling battery technology would have an edge. For years, that vision seemed early. Now, it looks increasingly prescient.

## The Road Ahead

BYD’s transformation from battery supplier to global EV contender reflects a broader shift in the auto industry. The center of gravity is moving toward electrification, software and supply-chain control — areas where China has invested heavily.

For legacy automakers, BYD represents a new kind of competitor: one that did not begin with engines, transmissions or a century of brand heritage, but with cells, chemistry and manufacturing scale.

For Wang Chuanfu, the next challenge may be the hardest yet. BYD has already helped change how cars are made and powered in China. Now it wants to prove it can win over drivers around the world.

(CNN) -- Before BYD became one of the world’s most closely watched electric-vehicle makers, it was a battery company operating out of Shenzhen, the fast-growing manufacturing hub that helped define China’s export boom.

Founded in 1995 by chemist and entrepreneur Wang Chuanfu, BYD — short for “Build Your Dreams” — began by making rechargeable batteries for mobile phones and consumer electronics. Its early advantage was not built on expensive automation, but on a labor-intensive manufacturing model that used large teams of workers to perform tasks that rivals in Japan and South Korea often assigned to costly machines.

That strategy helped BYD keep costs low, scale quickly and compete with established battery producers. Wang’s approach reflected a broader ambition: to show that Chinese manufacturers could move beyond low-cost assembly and become global technology leaders.

“Made in China should not mean cheap and low quality,” Wang has said in remarks about the company’s rise. “It should mean innovation, reliability and responsibility.”

BYD’s move into automobiles came in 2003, when it purchased Qinchuan Automobile, a small state-owned carmaker in Xi’an. The acquisition gave BYD a foothold in the auto industry and paved the way for the creation of BYD Auto. At the time, the decision surprised some observers: a battery maker was stepping into one of the world’s most capital-intensive and competitive businesses.

But Wang saw batteries and vehicles as increasingly connected. As global concern grew over oil consumption, air pollution and climate change, BYD invested heavily in electric cars, plug-in hybrids and energy-storage technologies.

“We have a responsibility to use technology to help solve environmental problems,” Wang has said. “A company cannot only think about profit; it must also think about the future of society.”

Today, BYD’s origins remain central to its identity. Its battery expertise became the foundation for its electric-vehicle push, while its Shenzhen roots placed it at the center of China’s manufacturing transformation. The company’s rise from a small battery producer to a major automaker reflects both Wang’s unconventional methods and China’s broader effort to redefine what “Made in China” means in the global economy.

**BYD: The battery maker driving China’s electric car ambitions**

*CNN-style business news story*

SHENZHEN, China — In a country determined to move from factory floor to technological powerhouse, few companies better capture Beijing’s industrial ambitions than BYD.

Founded by Wang Chuanfu, a chemist-turned-entrepreneur, BYD began in the 1990s making rechargeable batteries for mobile phones. Today, it is one of China’s most closely watched automakers and a symbol of the country’s push to dominate the next generation of transportation: electric vehicles.

BYD’s rise reflects the transformation of China’s auto market, now the world’s largest. Once dominated by foreign joint ventures and gasoline-powered models, the market has rapidly shifted toward electrification, supported by government subsidies, aggressive industrial policy, and growing consumer acceptance of Chinese brands.

The company’s early expertise in batteries gave it a crucial advantage as electric vehicles moved from niche product to mainstream business. Unlike many traditional automakers, BYD developed much of its battery technology in-house, allowing it to compete on cost and scale while positioning itself as both a carmaker and a clean-energy company.

Its global profile received a major boost in 2008, when Warren Buffett’s Berkshire Hathaway invested about $250 million in BYD through its MidAmerican Energy unit. The endorsement from one of the world’s most famous investors gave BYD credibility far beyond China and signaled that electric vehicles were becoming a serious long-term bet.

Still, BYD’s ascent has not been without skepticism. Chinese manufacturers have long faced concerns overseas about product quality, safety standards and brand reliability. For BYD and other Chinese automakers, winning international consumers will require proving that their vehicles can match global competitors not only on price, but also on performance, durability and trust.

At home, however, BYD has become a national champion — a company that embodies China’s hopes of leapfrogging established automotive powers. As global demand for electric vehicles accelerates, BYD is no longer just a battery maker from Shenzhen. It is now a central player in the race to define the future of the car industry.
